subject: history

moments.title: Lenin returns in a sealed train
moments.body: The German government provides a sealed train through Germany to Sweden, calculating that Lenin will destabilise Russia and take it out of the war. Lenin arrives at the Finland Station, Petrograd, on 16 April and issues the April Theses — 'all power to the Soviets', no support for the Provisional Government, immediate peace.
moments.takeaway: German intelligence calculated correctly. By November the Bolsheviks had seized power and signed a separate peace (Brest-Litovsk, March 1918).

moments.title: The October Revolution
moments.who: The Bolsheviks under Lenin and Trotsky
moments.body: On 7 November (25 October OS), Bolshevik forces seize the Winter Palace in Petrograd. Trotsky organises the Military Revolutionary Committee. Kerensky flees. The Bolsheviks issue the Decree on Peace and the Decree on Land within hours.
moments.takeaway: The 'storming' of the Winter Palace was largely a Soviet propaganda image (especially Eisenstein's 1928 film). The actual takeover was smaller and less dramatic — but no less consequential.

now.title: The shadow of 1917
now.body: The Soviet Union lasted 74 years. The Cold War, Mao's revolution in China (1949), Castro's in Cuba (1959), Vietnam, the entire 20th-century communist project — all trace back to that November in Petrograd. The collapse of 1991 closed one cycle; Putin's reading of Russian history (his 'greatest geopolitical catastrophe' line) opens another.
now.open_questions: Was October 1917 a coup or a revolution? Soviet historiography insisted on revolution. Western Cold War scholarship often called it a coup. Sheila Fitzpatrick and Stephen Kotkin have argued for more nuanced 'revolution from above with popular elements' framings.

reflection: Revolutions don't happen because of one cause. War, famine, a discredited monarchy, a weak provisional government, a disciplined party with a plausible programme — Russia in 1917 had all of them.
